note.explanation: Mass tells us how much matter an object contains and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on the object, so it can change when gravitational field strength changes.
examples: A person with a mass of 80 kg has a weight of 800 N on Earth when g = 10 N kg⁻¹.
The same person has a weight of 128 N on the Moon when g = 1.6 m s⁻².
note.checkAnswer: Mass is measured in kilograms and stays the same; weight is a gravitational force measured in newtons and can change with g.
note.simple: Mass is how much matter is in something. Weight is the pull of gravity on it.
note.checkQuestion: What is the weight of a 2 kg object where g = 10 N kg⁻¹?
note.title: Mass and Weight
steps: Put in the mass and the value of g.
Multiply to find the weight, and give the answer in newtons.
note.answer: Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object: w = mg.

written.text: A 10 kg block moves on a frictionless horizontal surface with an acceleration of 2 m s⁻². What is the force acting on the block?

rubric.why: The correct law connects force, mass and acceleration.
The given values must be substituted correctly.
rubric.how: Use m = 10 kg and a = 2 m s⁻².

rubric.why: The result and its unit complete the calculation.
rubric.how: Calculate 10 × 2 and state the answer in newtons.

modelAnswer: Mass of a block = m = 10 kg
By Newton's second law of motion, F = ma
Putting the values, F = 10 kg × 2 m s⁻² = 20 kg m s⁻² = 20 N

written.text: A force of 7500 N is applied to move a truck of mass 3000 kg. Find the acceleration produced in the truck. How long will it take to accelerate the truck from 36 km h⁻¹ to 72 km h⁻¹ speed?

rubric.why: The speeds must be converted to SI units before using the motion equation.
rubric.description: Convert both speeds to metres per second.
rubric.how: Show that 36 km h⁻¹ = 10 m s⁻¹ and 72 km h⁻¹ = 20 m s⁻¹.

rubric.why: Newton's second law gives the truck's acceleration.
rubric.description: Calculate acceleration from force and mass.

rubric.why: The first equation of motion is needed to find the time.
rubric.description: Use the first equation of motion.
rubric.how: Rearrange v_f = v_i + at to find t.

rubric.why: The final time must be calculated correctly and include its unit.

modelAnswer: Final speed = v_f = 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000 m / (60 × 60 s) = 20 m s⁻¹
By Newton's second law, F = ma
Putting the values, a = 7500 N / 3000 kg = 2.5 m s⁻²
Now, using first equation of motion, v_f = v_i + at
Putting the values, t = (20 m s⁻¹ − 10 m s⁻¹) / 2.5 m s⁻² = 4 s

explain.title: Mass
explain.body: The simplest definition of mass is that it is a measure of the quantity of matter in a body. Scientifically, mass is a scalar quantity and remains the same everywhere. Its SI unit is kilogram (kg), and an ordinary balance measures mass.

explain.title: Scientific definition of mass
explain.body: The characteristic of a body which determines the magnitude of acceleration produced when a certain force acts upon it is known as mass of the body.

explain.title: Weight
explain.body: Weight is a gravitational force acting on the object. It is a vector quantity directed downward, towards the centre of the Earth. The weight of an object is equal to the force with which the Earth attracts the body towards its centre.

explain.title: Gravitational field and weight
explain.body: The gravitational field is a space around a mass in which another mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction. The gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force acting on unit mass. Weight is given by w = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength. Its value is 10 N kg⁻¹. Since g varies from place to place and with altitude, weight can change; mass stays the same. Weight is measured in newtons (N) using a spring balance.

mistakes: Do not say that an object's weight is measured in kilograms; kilograms are the unit of mass and newtons are the unit of weight.
Do not treat mass and weight as the same quantity: mass is scalar and stays the same, while weight is a vector force that depends on g.
Do not use Earth's value of g when a question gives a different value, such as the Moon's gravitational acceleration.
Do not omit the unit N from a calculated weight.
